book.title: Factfulness
book.author: Hans Rosling, Ola Rosling, Anna Rosling Rönnlund

chapters.title: The Gap Instinct
chapters.hook: Hans Rosling's bubble chart shows why the old rich/poor split missed the 68% in the middle.
chapters.counterintuition: It feels clear to split the world into rich and poor. Rosling's correction is that the split often hides the crowded middle, where most lives and many changes sit.
chapters.tryThisNow: When a country label or headline comes up today, pause before you answer. Ask where most people are, then ask whether the label is older than the data.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Before judging the world by its extremes, locate the middle, check movement over time, and use income levels as a rough ladder rather than old two-box labels.

breakdown.fastRead:
Rosling's old bubble chart begins with a real split: in 1965, many countries sat in a low-survival, high-fertility box. The picture looks like two worlds. Then the 2017 chart arrives, and the clean split breaks. Many bubbles have moved into the middle or upper range.

The gap instinct is the habit of cutting the world into two camps and picturing an empty space between them. It feels tidy. It is often false. The gap is often a bad map.

Use Find the Middle, a quick check that asks where the largest group sits before you name the whole world: ask where most people are before the loud extremes take over. Keep severe poverty in view, but do not let it stand for everyone outside rich countries.
breakdown.deepRead:
A line on a chart can make a crowd disappear. When the mind sees two clumps, it wants two names. Developed and developing sound practical, but they train the eye to expect a gulf. In 1965, that picture had some visual support. By 2017, the bubbles no longer fit the old split.

Cover the labels on the 2017 health chart and the old words become harder to defend. The old words say two camps. The dots say movement. Some countries still face harsh child mortality and poverty. Many others sit between the poorest and the richest, with better survival, smaller families, and uneven but real gains.

That is why Rosling's four income levels matter. They are a rough ladder of daily income, not a rank of human worth. Level 1: less than $2 per day. Level 2: $2-$8 per day. Level 3: $8-$32 per day. Level 4: more than $32 per day. A family on Level 2 may have a bicycle but no steady water. A family on Level 3 may have a motorbike and a fridge. Most people live between the drama.

This does not make the world fine. It makes the map usable. If you start with the poorest and richest pictures, you may miss the billions whose lives are neither disaster nor comfort. Find the Middle asks for one extra step before judgment: locate the crowd, then look at the edges.
breakdown.fullRead:
Put Sweden 1869 beside Saudi Arabia 1960 and the old ranking starts to wobble. The numbers feel shocking: 249 and 242 child deaths per 1,000 births. If the comparison stops there, the story can sound like national character: one country ahead, the other behind.

The dates change the story. Sweden needed 77 years, from 1869 to 1946, to get below 35 child deaths per 1,000 births. Saudi Arabia made a similar move from 1960 to 1993, in 33 years. The old gap picture turns into a moving road. Later starters can move faster because knowledge, vaccines, sanitation, and basic health systems already exist.

This is the heart of the idea. A false gap freezes people in place. A moving scale lets you see progress and pain at the same time. Saudi Arabia's faster change does not erase grief in the years when children died. Sweden's earlier progress does not make it a different kind of human society. It means both places moved through time, with different tools available.

World Bank language shows the same trap in official clothes. In a filmed World Bank lecture in June 2015, the old phrase developing world came under pressure because the data no longer matched it well. A later World Bank blog announced plans to phase that wording out. Old labels can outlive old facts.

Four levels can also be misused. If you treat them as fixed castes, you have only traded two boxes for four. The stronger habit is to see a road. Households can move up or down. People inside one country can live on different levels. A national average can hide a city apartment, a rural farm, and a family one illness away from falling.

A short news brief shows where the ladder can still mislead. The headline says a country is rising, but the chart shows one city on Level 4 and many villages near Level 2. The average is true and still thin. It cannot tell whose water is safe, whose clinic has medicine, or whose daughter can reach school.

Here is where Find the Middle breaks down: it cannot tell you what a specific family can afford tonight. A mother deciding whether to buy medicine or food needs local facts, not a global ladder. The ladder helps when you are tempted to say the world is split in two. It fails when a real person needs a price, a clinic, a school, or a safe road.

So use the tool for the right job. When a headline, map, or speech divides people into two camps, pause before you nod. Ask where the bubbles cluster. Ask whether the gap still exists. Ask whether the words are older than the facts. A better map does not make hardship smaller. It keeps hardship from being placed in the wrong world.

examples.title: The Bubble Chart Split
examples.scenario: At 8:00 a.m., a teacher in the Gapminder training room marks bubble chart 1-1; Rosling's 1965 chart shows many countries in a low-survival, high-fertility box. The 2017 chart spreads the bubbles upward and inward, so the old two-world label no longer describes where most people live.
examples.whatToDo: Show the two charts in order. Name the old split, then ask where the 2017 bubbles cluster before choosing a label.
examples.whyItMatters: The move keeps history and update together. Readers learn to ask whether a category still fits before they reuse it.

examples.title: Sweden and Saudi Arabia by Time
examples.scenario: At 8:01 a.m., a teacher in the Gapminder training room marks bubble chart 1-2; Sweden moved from 249 child deaths per 1,000 births in 1869 to below 35 in 1946. Saudi Arabia moved from 242 in 1960 to a similar level in 1993. The useful comparison is not rank; it is timing, tools, and pace.
examples.whatToDo: Keep the death rates and years on the same page so the comparison turns from national status into historical movement.
examples.whyItMatters: The exchange makes the gap instinct less automatic. A country can look far away when the real difference is timing, tools, and speed of change.

examples.title: The World Bank Label Lag
examples.scenario: At 8:02 a.m., a teacher in the Gapminder training room marks bubble chart 1-3; In a June 2015 World Bank lecture, the phrase developing world no longer fit the data well. A later World Bank blog described phasing out that wording. The language trailed the facts.
examples.whatToDo: Treat official wording as evidence to check, not proof that the old map is current.
examples.whyItMatters: Institutions can keep useful but stale words alive. Readers need to compare official terms with the distribution those terms claim to name.

examples.title: The 1965 and 2017 Thread
examples.scenario: At 8:03 a.m., a teacher in the Gapminder training room marks bubble chart 1-4; A 1965 chart can still make two worlds feel obvious. Send the 2017 chart next and the question changes: where did the middle go? The answer is that it was there in the bubbles, not in the old label.
examples.whatToDo: Use the second chart to locate the largest group before naming the world.
examples.whyItMatters: Fast messages reward simple labels. A second chart and one middle-seeking question can slow the reflex before it hardens.

examples.title: The Child-Mortality Scale
examples.scenario: At 8:04 a.m., a teacher in the Gapminder training room marks bubble chart 1-5; A rank-order exercise breaks when Sweden 1869-1946 and Saudi Arabia 1960-1993 sit near the same child-mortality rates but move on different calendars.
examples.whatToDo: Redraw the comparison as movement over time, with the years visible.
examples.whyItMatters: The pause is the method. Changing the layout helps a reader see a moving road instead of a fixed ladder of countries.

examples.title: The Four-Level Napkin
examples.scenario: At 8:05 a.m., a teacher in the Gapminder training room marks bubble chart 1-6; The four income levels are a rough daily-income ladder: Level 1 below $2, Level 2 $2-$8, Level 3 $8-$32, Level 4 above $32. They improve on two boxes but still need local detail.
examples.whatToDo: Explain each rung as a working map, then ask what a national average hides.
examples.whyItMatters: A small wording edit can change the reader's map. The levels show rough positions without pretending every country is one thing.

questions.prompt: A manager at a board review applies the gap instinct before answering. The teacher sees the 1965 chart split into two clusters, then checks 2017. Which reading fits the later chart?
choices: The older two-box wording still fits because it once matched a visible chart pattern.
The chart mainly proves that country labels should replace income and health data.
The old split hides many countries that moved into overlapping middle positions.
questions.explanation: Fact 1 supports the 2017 overlap. A 1965 visual split should not be reused as if it still described most people.

questions.prompt: A teacher with a marked worksheet uses the gap instinct for this case. Two presenters compare Sweden 1869 with Saudi Arabia 1960. Which conclusion follows from the child mortality numbers?
choices: Both cases show movement over time, and Saudi Arabia made a similar drop faster.
Both cases show that countries need the same number of years to improve.
Both cases show that early national rank predicts a fixed health future.
questions.explanation: Fact 2 says both moved from roughly 240 to 250 deaths per 1,000 to below 35, with Saudi Arabia moving faster.

questions.prompt: A report opens with the poorest and richest photos. What should the presenter check before drawing a global conclusion?
choices: Whether the photos show the most dramatic cases at both ends of the scale.
Whether the richest group can be used as the main sign of progress.
Where the majority sits, since vivid extremes can distort normal life.
questions.explanation: Fact 3 points to the majority before the extremes. The poorest and richest groups are real, but they do not define normal global life.

questions.prompt: A student comparing two notes tries the gap instinct here. The class replaces rich and poor with four income levels. Which use of that ladder matches the source data?
choices: The four levels give the same split a kinder name while keeping two camps in place.
The four levels show gradual material differences inside and across countries.
The four levels prove that every household in a nation shares one standard.
questions.explanation: Fact 4 supports the ladder because it shows middle positions. The common error is treating four levels as a softer binary.

questions.prompt: A founder editing a briefing tests the gap instinct against the options. A World Bank phrase survives after the chart has changed. Which lesson should Isabelle take from the wording shift?
choices: Official language may update quickly while public habits keep using the older phrase.
Official language can lag behind the data it is meant to describe.
Official language is a safer guide than charts when categories conflict.
questions.explanation: Fact 5 points to lag. The World Bank wording mattered because an institution can preserve an old category after the distribution changes.

questions.prompt: A parent reading a school handout practices the gap instinct on this example. A data table mixes extreme poverty with rich-country poverty lines. Which distinction keeps the numbers honest?
choices: Extreme poverty uses a far lower global line than many rich-country poverty measures.
Extreme poverty and rich-country poverty use the same dollar line everywhere.
Extreme poverty is measured only by national labels rather than household income.
questions.explanation: Fact 6 separates the measures. The global extreme-poverty line sits far below many rich-country relative poverty thresholds.

questions.prompt: A coach preparing a short lesson checks the gap instinct in the situation. A reader changes a chart from child mortality to child survival. What has changed in the reader's view?
choices: The chart now uses a new data source, so the old numbers no longer count.
The same data now frames movement upward, which can make progress easier to see.
The chart now removes hardship by changing the wording on the axis.
questions.explanation: Fact 7 says the data stay the same while the frame changes. Survival wording can reduce misreading without changing the facts.

questions.prompt: A director revising a memo brings the gap instinct to the choice. A country average looks tidy on one line. Which warning follows from the four-level map?
choices: Averages should be set aside whenever a single household story is available.
Averages work best when every household is assigned the national level.
Averages can hide households on different levels inside the same country.
questions.explanation: Fact 8 warns that people inside one country can live on different levels. Averages are useful, but they can compress internal differences.

questions.prompt: A vp scanning a dashboard uses the gap instinct before picking an answer. The editor says the correction is to be more hopeful. Which reply keeps the hard edge of this idea?
choices: The correction is to inspect the distribution before judging progress or hardship.
The correction is to say the world is mostly fine and stop stressing poverty.
The correction is to focus on the worst cases because they are most vivid.
questions.explanation: Fact 9 says the cure is distributions, not positivity. This method keeps severe poverty visible while rejecting a false empty gap.

reviewCards.front: What does the gap instinct make the world look like?
reviewCards.back: It makes humanity look split into two camps with an empty gulf between them. That picture hides the large middle where many people live and move.

reviewCards.front: Why are four income levels better than rich versus poor?
reviewCards.back: Because rich versus poor splits the world into a false gap. Four levels show material life as a ladder of steps, not two boxes. Level 1 is less than $2 per day, Level 2 is $2-$8, Level 3 is $8-$32, and Level 4 is more than $32 per day.

reviewCards.front: What do Sweden and Saudi Arabia teach about child mortality?
reviewCards.back: They show that high child mortality is not a fixed national type. Both moved from roughly 240 to 250 deaths per 1,000 births to below 35, but Saudi Arabia moved faster.

reviewCards.front: What does the World Bank wording change warn you to check?
reviewCards.back: Check whether an official phrase still matches the data. The phrase developing world lingered even as the distribution had moved beyond a clean two-box map.

reviewCards.front: What is the difference between Find the Middle and optimism?
reviewCards.back: Find the Middle asks where people actually cluster before judging. It does not say hardship is gone; it keeps severe poverty visible without letting extremes define everyone.

implementationPlan.title: Find the Middle First
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice catching a two-box story before it becomes your map. Use Find the Middle: locate the largest group, check movement over time, then ask whether an old label still fits the data.

ifThenPlans.context: Dramatic examples
ifThenPlans.plan: If a report opens with the poorest and richest cases, then ask where most people sit before you treat either end as normal.

ifThenPlans.context: Official wording
ifThenPlans.plan: If a speech or memo uses a familiar global label, then check whether the distribution has changed since that label became common.

ifThenPlans.context: Country averages
ifThenPlans.plan: If one national number seems to explain everyone, then look for households on different income levels inside the country.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Pick the next chart, headline, or map that crosses your desk and find its middle first; swap one broad label for a level, a trend, or a distribution.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: At the end of this week, review one conversation where you used Find the Middle. Name what changed about your map: the largest group, the time trend, or the label you dropped.

memorableLines.text: Most people are often between the extremes.
memorableLines.why: It turns the chapter's warning into a short test of a visual split.

memorableLines.text: Income levels are a rough ladder, not a verdict.
memorableLines.why: It makes the middle easy to remember when extremes pull attention.

memorableLines.text: Old labels can outlive old facts.
memorableLines.why: It captures the World Bank wording lesson in a portable line.

chapters.title: The Negativity Instinct
chapters.hook: The news gives us blood up front and slow gains in the margins.
chapters.counterintuition: Bad news feels like proof of decline because sudden harm is vivid. Rosling's question is plainer: is the current level bad, and which way is the line moving?
chapters.tryThisNow: At your next news scan, mark each frightening item with two notes: current level and trend. If you do not know the trend, write that.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Bad news should start a Trend Check: name the level, name the trend, and ask whether a loud event is hiding quiet long-run change.

breakdown.fastRead:
Hans Rosling points to Eriksberg in Uppsala, Sweden, near the Ekeby brick factory. The sanitation was rough into the postwar decades, and big fixes did not arrive until the 1970s. Rich-country comfort is recent.

The negativity instinct is the habit of noticing loss faster than slow improvement. It then makes a fast jump: bad news means decline. Bad news is a signal, not a verdict. Ask two questions first. How bad is the level right now? Which way has the trend moved? A trend can improve and still describe pain.
breakdown.deepRead:
The Global Terrorism Database makes the lesson harder than simple cheerfulness. Terrorism deaths sat near a low of about 2,200 in 1999. By 2014 the count had risen to 32,765, then declined somewhat. The honest response is: we cannot say everything is better. We can say this indicator got worse, and still test other indicators on their own charts.

That is the mechanism. Bad events arrive as scenes: a bombing, a spill, a closed ward, a flooded street. Progress often arrives as a thinner line on a chart: fewer children dying, fewer oil spill accidents, fewer people in extreme poverty. The mind remembers the scene and misses the line. Progress is not comfort; it is direction.

Trend Check means separating current level from direction of change. It protects two truths at once. First, the level may be awful. A high child mortality rate is not good because it fell. Second, the trend may still matter. If the rate keeps falling across many sources, that tells workers, voters, and donors that some methods helped. The same logic handles uncertainty. The old extreme-poverty estimates are not perfect, but they can still show a strong downward direction. Trend thinking is not cheerfulness. It is a guardrail against despair and denial.
breakdown.fullRead:
Rosling's Eriksberg example makes the negativity instinct local. The old sanitation conditions were not safely parked in some distant country. They were Sweden within living memory, near the Ekeby brickworks in Uppsala, with major improvements arriving late enough to embarrass a simple rich-country story.

That changes the lesson. The negativity instinct is not only a taste for grim headlines. It is also amnesia. People forget how recently their own streets, toilets, clinics, and pay packets were worse. When hardship is placed far away, progress starts to sound like a polite story about strangers. Uppsala pulls it back home.

A weekly news scan shows the same trap. The first draft is all alarm: terrorism, dead zones, threatened species, and fish stocks under pressure. None of those worries is fake. The source keeps them in the picture. Environmental decline is not a media trick. The terrorism data set is not a mood swing. Some lines move the wrong way.

The better draft adds the missing column. Extreme poverty fell over the long run, even with doubt around older estimates. Child mortality fell across UN-IGME and historical sources. Oil spill accidents became much rarer after the 1970s. Smallpox ended after WHO vaccination work and the last known case in Somalia in 1977. The page is not happier. It is fuller.

Trend Check means reading four things before drawing the mood of the world: current level, direction, reliability, and visibility. A high current level may still be terrible. A downward trend may still matter. A worsening line should not be hidden inside a progress speech. A noisy headline should not be mistaken for the whole table.

The cost is real. A short speech saying the world is safer than people think would be easier to give. The data will not allow it. The 1999 terrorism low and the 2014 spike have to sit in the same chapter as the improvement charts. The sentence becomes less neat and more useful.

That is the Rosling tone at its best: serious about suffering, allergic to despair as a shortcut. To use the Trend Check well, give up the rush of one pure story. Keep the bad level, keep the improving trend when it is there, and keep the cases that do not improve.

examples.title: Eriksberg in Uppsala
examples.scenario: At 8:06 a.m., an editor in the Uppsala library room marks trend memo 2-1; Eriksberg near Uppsala's Ekeby brick factory reminds rich-country readers that rough sanitation was not some distant foreign condition. In Rosling's account, big fixes arrived late enough to challenge modern amnesia.
examples.whatToDo: Put the place and date back into the story before poverty becomes a label for somewhere else.
examples.whyItMatters: The repair makes progress local. When readers remember that rich countries changed recently, they are less likely to treat today's hardship elsewhere as fixed.

examples.title: The Terrorism Line That Worsened
examples.scenario: At 8:07 a.m., an editor in the Uppsala library room marks trend memo 2-2; The Global Terrorism Database does not support a simple happy story: about 2,200 deaths in 1999, 32,765 in 2014, then some decline. One worsening line should not be hidden inside an improvement slogan.
examples.whatToDo: Name the bad rise and use it as a warning to test each indicator on its own chart.
examples.whyItMatters: The memo keeps honesty from becoming despair. A real counterexample should sharpen the Trend Check, not cancel the whole habit of checking trends.

examples.title: Doubt Plus Direction
examples.scenario: At 8:08 a.m., an editor in the Uppsala library room marks trend memo 2-3; Older extreme-poverty counts carry uncertainty, yet a long fall can still be visible across sources. The honest reading keeps both facts: imperfect levels and a strong direction.
examples.whatToDo: Keep one column for measurement doubt and one for direction of change.
examples.whyItMatters: This keeps care from getting stuck. Uncertainty can humble a number without erasing the direction that tells people which efforts may be working.

examples.title: Level, Trend, Unknown
examples.scenario: At 8:09 a.m., an editor in the Uppsala library room marks trend memo 2-4; Terrorism, dead zones, threatened species, and fish stocks under pressure are serious. The Trend Check asks whether each item is a bad level, a worsening trend, an improving trend, or still unknown.
examples.whatToDo: Label each item before turning the news feed into a single story of collapse.
examples.whyItMatters: The reframe gives the reader a clean pause. It lets concern stay sharp while the Trend Check decides what kind of evidence is on the table.

examples.title: Imperfect Counts, Useful Direction
examples.scenario: At 8:10 a.m., an editor in the Uppsala library room marks trend memo 2-5; Child mortality and oil-spill accident charts do not need perfect old measurements to teach direction. The claim is narrower: several long-run lines moved down.
examples.whatToDo: Say what the chart can claim and what it cannot claim.
examples.whyItMatters: The learner's confusion is useful. It teaches readers to respect doubt without letting doubt become an excuse to ignore every long-run improvement.

examples.title: The Partial Failure Meeting
examples.scenario: At 8:11 a.m., an editor in the Uppsala library room marks trend memo 2-6; A meeting led only with the 2014 terrorism death count and other alarming items may produce heat but little clarity. A second meeting can keep the same concerns while requiring level, trend, and source before reaction.
examples.whatToDo: Change the process, not the concern.
examples.whyItMatters: The before-after view shows the cost of missing slow gains. Bad news still matters, but it no longer gets to stand in for the whole world.

questions.prompt: A chart shows extreme poverty falling over many decades, while many families still live with serious hardship. Which reading best resists the negativity instinct?
choices: The fall shows real progress, and the remaining hardship still deserves action.
The fall shows the problem has mostly left the serious category.
The hardship shows the chart cannot count as real progress.
questions.explanation: Factfulness keeps level and trend apart. A condition can improve and still be bad. Choice 1 treats improvement as solved; choice 2 treats remaining harm as proof that progress is fake.

questions.prompt: The visitor hears that Eriksberg in Uppsala still had sanitation problems into the postwar decades. What should that change in her picture?
choices: Rich-country comfort is recent enough that today's hardship elsewhere should not be treated as a fixed foreign state.
Sweden was already far removed from Level 2 hardship, so Eriksberg is mainly a strange local exception.
Uppsala's past proves all countries will follow the same time path toward comfort.
questions.explanation: The Eriksberg case shows that conditions now seen as foreign existed recently in a rich country. Choice 1 keeps the old distance; choice 2 turns one local memory into a rigid forecast.

questions.prompt: The Global Terrorism Database shows deaths near 2,200 in 1999 and 32,765 in 2014. Which response best matches the Trend Check?
choices: Treat the rise as a detail that should be folded into the same improvement story as other indicators.
Treat the rise as proof that claims about wider human progress should be dismissed.
Treat the rise as a real worsening line inside a mixed picture that still needs separate trend checks.
questions.explanation: Terrorism is the check against blanket optimism. It worsened over that span. The right move is to keep it real while checking other indicators on their own evidence.

questions.prompt: Two readers see warnings about fish stocks, dead zones, and threatened species. Which reader is applying the Trend Check more carefully?
choices: The reader who says negative stories are usually media bias and should be discounted first.
The reader who says any environmental warning cancels the need to inspect improvement charts.
The reader who keeps the warnings as real evidence while still checking each trend separately.
questions.explanation: The source keeps environmental decline in the picture. Negativity is not always illusion. Choice 0 dismisses real harm; choice 1 lets one warning erase all other trend work.

questions.prompt: A reviewer says old extreme-poverty estimates are uncertain, so the long-run fall cannot teach anything. What is the best reply?
choices: Uncertain estimates should be ignored until every past level can be measured exactly.
Uncertainty can blur exact levels while still leaving a clear long-run direction.
Uncertainty makes the trend useful only as a story, not as evidence.
questions.explanation: The fact supports direction despite uncertainty. Exact old levels may be fuzzy, but consistent methods can still show a fall. The other choices turn doubt into total denial.

questions.prompt: In the instructor's data class, a student points at the child mortality chart and says the past is too hard to measure. Which answer fits the source?
choices: The measures are too mixed to support a useful comparison across long periods.
The estimates are imperfect, but overlapping sources still support a sustained global fall.
The decline can be trusted only in countries with modern hospital records.
questions.explanation: The sidecar points to UN-IGME and historical compilations showing a long fall. The source does not claim perfect measurement; it says the direction is well supported.

questions.prompt: A log of large tanker accidents shows an average of 24.5 per year in the 1970s and 1.7 per year in 2010-2016. What should the reader infer?
choices: Modern industry has made oil spill accidents more common decade by decade.
The numbers are too far apart in time to say anything about direction.
Large tanker accidents became much rarer after the 1970s.
questions.explanation: The ITOPF figures support a clear drop in average accident count. Choice 0 reverses the trend; choice 1 rejects a direction the cited numbers are strong enough to show.

questions.prompt: During a review of disease trends, the organizer says no human disease has ever been ended worldwide. Which correction is grounded in the source?
choices: Smallpox declined in many countries but remained outside the global-eradication column.
WHO vaccination campaigns ended smallpox after the last known case in Somalia in 1977.
Smallpox faded mainly because living standards rose, not because vaccination ended it.
questions.explanation: The source names smallpox as a real global improvement tied to WHO vaccination work and the last known case in Somalia in 1977. The other choices deny or replace that mechanism.

questions.prompt: A news feed shows sudden disasters all morning and no stories about small annual gains. Which first conclusion fits the negativity instinct?
choices: Bad events are more reportable than quiet gains, so the feed alone cannot prove decline.
Bad events dominate the feed because slow gains usually stop during crisis periods.
Bad events should be treated as better evidence because they are easier to verify.
questions.explanation: News favors drama. That means an improving world can still produce a grim feed. The other choices mistake visibility for trend evidence or make bad events more reliable by default.

reviewCards.front: What does the Trend Check ask you to run after bad news?
reviewCards.back: Name the current level, name the trend, check how reliable the data is, and ask whether sudden news is louder than slow change. This keeps concern from turning into a false story of decline.

reviewCards.front: How can a condition be improving and still demand action?
reviewCards.back: Level and trend answer different questions. A falling child mortality rate is progress, but a high rate still means children are dying and work remains urgent.

reviewCards.front: Why does the Global Terrorism Database keep the negativity lesson from becoming optimism?
reviewCards.back: It shows a real worsening line: deaths rose from the 1999 low to a much higher 2014 level. Factfulness allows bad reversals inside a broader mixed picture.

reviewCards.front: In one sentence, how do you connect the gap instinct (Ch 1) to the Trend Check?
reviewCards.back: The gap instinct asks where most people sit instead of staring at extremes; the negativity instinct asks where the trend moves instead of staring only at bad events.

reviewCards.front: What should uncertainty about old extreme-poverty data change, and what should it not change?
reviewCards.back: It should make the exact past level feel less crisp. It should not erase a strong long-run fall when consistent methods still point in the same direction.

implementationPlan.title: Run a Trend Check
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice the Trend Check when bad news makes decline feel obvious. Say the level, say the trend, then ask whether a loud event is crowding out slow change. The skill is not cheerfulness; it is holding bad levels and better trends in the same hand.

ifThenPlans.context: When a news feed makes the whole world feel worse
ifThenPlans.plan: If the feed is all sudden harm, then pause and ask for one trend line before you state a conclusion.

ifThenPlans.context: When someone says improvement means the problem is solved
ifThenPlans.plan: If a falling line gets treated as solved, then name the current level and the people still hurt by it.

ifThenPlans.context: When one indicator truly worsens
ifThenPlans.plan: If a real worsening line appears, then keep it on the page and check other indicators separately.

ifThenPlans.context: When data uncertainty becomes a reason to ignore a trend
ifThenPlans.plan: If the exact old number is fuzzy, then ask whether the direction still holds across the best available sources.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Keep a tally on your phone today: one mark each time bad news makes you assume decline without first checking its level and trend. That running tally is the Trend Check in action.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Across this week, tally each time you hear or make an "everything is getting worse" claim. At week's end, read the number and pick one claim to Trend Check aloud.

memorableLines.text: Bad news starts a check; it does not finish the story.
memorableLines.why: It turns the chapter into a pause the reader can use.

memorableLines.text: A trend can improve and still describe pain.
memorableLines.why: It keeps progress and urgency together in one short sentence.

memorableLines.text: Uncertainty about old levels does not erase every direction.
memorableLines.why: It warns against treating improvement as permission to relax.

chapters.title: The Straight Line Instinct
chapters.hook: Two child-count forecasts, 1.975 billion in 2017 and 1.957 billion in 2100, undercut the simple baby-boom fear.
chapters.counterintuition: A straight line is not a forecast. It is a ruler laid across a living system, and the system may already be changing.
chapters.tryThisNow: The next time a graph or rising number comes up, write BEND in the margin. Name the force that would keep it straight before you trust the line.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Before you extend a trend, ask what shape the line could take, what force could bend it, and whether the visible window is too small.

breakdown.fastRead:
Start with two child counts from the UN WPP 2017 forecast: 1.975 billion in 2017 and 1.957 billion in 2100. The UN WPP 2017 line does not show endless babies. It rises toward a peak around 2057, then comes back near where it began.

The straight line instinct is the habit of extending the latest slope as if nothing can bend it. Population can still grow while the child count stays almost flat. Adults, not babies, carry much of this forecast.

Use Bend Check, a habit of asking what could change a line's shape: ask what kind of line you are seeing, then ask what could make it bend. Straight lines are guesses until causes earn them.
breakdown.deepRead:
A small piece of a chart can fool the eye. Jordan Ellenberg makes this plain with a circle lesson in How Not to Be Wrong: zoom in close enough and a curved edge looks like a line. A short window can make a curve look tame.

The same trick happens with births, income, vaccines, and consumption. The mind sees a recent rise and draws forward. That may work for a while. It fails when the reason for the rise changes. A vaccine rate can climb fast, then flatten as it nears most people. A product can spread in an S-bend. A harm can rise with income, then fall when rules and habits change. The shape belongs to the cause, not to the ruler.

The fertility line shows the trap. If a briefing shows only a short recent slice, families can seem locked into high birth rates. If it shows the longer line, the picture changes: global fertility moved from 5.05 children per woman in 1950 to 2.48 in 2017. That is not a tiny wiggle. It is a major bend in family size.

Bend Check asks for a cause before a line gets a future. The cause is the force in the world that makes the number rise, flatten, or fall. For fertility, the source refuses a single-cause story. Child survival matters. Education matters. Women's rights, lower poverty, and contraception matter too. When those forces change together, family choices change. The safe move is not to distrust every forecast. It is to ask which forces keep the line straight and which ones could turn it.
breakdown.fullRead:
Draw only a thumb-wide arc from a circle and it can look like a straight line. The mistake is not silly. Jordan Ellenberg's circle lesson is there because the eye is easy to trick. When the window is small, the ruler feels smarter than it is.

Forecasting is still useful. The UN Population Division still makes forecasts, and the 2017 medium variant is a careful one. Its child count sits near 1.975 billion for 2017 and near 1.957 billion for 2100, with a peak around 2057. The surprising part is what the forecast says about growth. Total population can rise while the number of children does not keep rising. Longer lives and age structure do much of the work.

This changes the fear picture. A person who imagines the future as a straight child line sees nurseries multiplying forever. The UN WPP 2017 story is different. Many children already born move into adult years. More adults survive into old age. The world's age stack changes even when births per woman fall.

Replacement fertility is another place where the neat number breaks. Two children per woman is not always replacement. The source gives a global replacement rate near 2.3, not exactly 2.0, because mortality matters. If more children and adults die before having children, a population needs a higher average to replace itself.

The hard part is that some lines really do stay straight for a useful stretch. Bend Check can become a lazy excuse if it turns every forecast into a shrug. The better rule is stricter. Ask for the mechanism. If the same force keeps pushing at the same pace, a straight projection may be fair. If survival improves, schooling spreads, rights change, poverty falls, contraception becomes available, a market fills up, or the view is too narrow, the ruler needs company.

A slope without a cause is only a drawing habit. That sentence is worth keeping near any chart that feels obvious. It does not tell you the right answer. It makes the next question harder to skip: what would make this line bend?

The same habit works outside population. A household can buy its first fridge once, not every year forever. A vaccination line can climb fast, then slow as it reaches the people left to reach. A road can be straight across one field and curve around the next hill. The line shape follows the forces in the world.

Do the opposite when the system is built to stay linear and the rule is fixed before the chart begins. If a contract says the payment rises by the same amount each month, do not invent a curve to look clever. Straight lines are allowed when the world has earned them. They are dangerous when they are only what the eye drew first.

examples.title: The UN Child Count
examples.scenario: At 8:12 a.m., a forecast writer in the Ellenberg seminar room marks population chart 3-1; UN WPP 2017 projected about 1.975 billion children in 2017 and about 1.957 billion in 2100, after a mid-century peak. Total population growth is therefore not the same as a rising number of children.
examples.whatToDo: Keep the two child counts visible and name age structure as the growth story.
examples.whyItMatters: The realization blocks the most tempting panic line. Readers learn to ask which age group is growing before they picture more babies forever.

examples.title: The Longer Fertility Line
examples.scenario: At 8:13 a.m., a forecast writer in the Ellenberg seminar room marks population chart 3-2; A short slice of fertility data can miss the bend. The longer line, from 5.05 children per woman in 1950 to 2.48 in 2017, shows a large change in family size.
examples.whatToDo: Use the longer chart when the audience needs the shape, not just the recent slope.
examples.whyItMatters: Planning attention is part of the method. A reader who sees the longer window is less likely to treat family size as fixed.

examples.title: Ellenberg's Circle Edge
examples.scenario: At 8:14 a.m., a forecast writer in the Ellenberg seminar room marks population chart 3-3; Jordan Ellenberg's circle lesson in How Not to Be Wrong shows why a curved edge can look straight when the window is tiny. The crop is the trap.
examples.whatToDo: Widen the view before extending the line.
examples.whyItMatters: The crop is not cosmetic. A small segment can make a reader trust a straight future that the full shape does not support.

examples.title: Age Structure, Not More Children
examples.scenario: At 8:15 a.m., a forecast writer in the Ellenberg seminar room marks population chart 3-4; The UN WPP 2017 forecast keeps the child count roughly flat while total population rises. The explanation is more adults and older people, not endless babies.
examples.whatToDo: Say the child counts aloud before describing the population forecast.
examples.whyItMatters: The exchange separates total population from child count. That protects readers from turning one rising line into the wrong rising line.

examples.title: The Fertility Reveal
examples.scenario: At 8:16 a.m., a forecast writer in the Ellenberg seminar room marks population chart 3-5; Covering the right side of the fertility chart invites the old guess that global fertility stayed near five children per woman. Revealing 2.48 in 2017 makes the bend visible.
examples.whatToDo: Let the wrong guess appear, then ask what life changes could bend the line.
examples.whyItMatters: The reveal makes the bend memorable. A number that surprises the room is harder to replace with the old fixed-family picture.

examples.title: The Wider Chart Reply
examples.scenario: At 8:17 a.m., a forecast writer in the Ellenberg seminar room marks population chart 3-6; A cropped chart that looks straight should trigger the Ellenberg warning: widen the view and ask what force would keep the slope straight.
examples.whatToDo: Replace the crop with the wider chart and one mechanism question.
examples.whyItMatters: The thread slows a fast mistake. A wider image and one cause question can stop a neat crop from becoming a false forecast.

questions.prompt: A forecast note says world population growth must mean ever more children. Which revision fits the UN WPP 2017 child line?
choices: The child count peaks near mid-century and ends close to its 2017 size.
The child count keeps climbing because total population keeps climbing.
The child count falls at once because fertility had already dropped by 2017.
questions.explanation: Fact 1 says the child population is projected to be about the same in 2100 as in 2017 after a mid-century peak. The other choices turn total growth into the wrong child story.

questions.prompt: Two readers see the same population projection. One counts births; the other checks age structure. Which reading best explains future growth?
choices: Growth comes only from higher fertility, so age structure adds little to the forecast.
Growth comes mainly from babies replacing adults, so survival changes matter less.
Growth comes largely from more people living into adult and older ages.
questions.explanation: Fact 2 points to age-structure momentum. More people surviving into adulthood and old age can lift total population even when births per woman fall.

questions.prompt: An engineer reading the chart applies the straight line instinct to the claim. A chart label says family size has stayed roughly constant worldwide. Which data reading should replace it?
choices: Global fertility stayed near 5 children per woman from 1950 through 2017.
Global fertility moved only slightly, so the straight line remains useful.
Global fertility fell from about 5.05 in 1950 to about 2.48 in 2017.
questions.explanation: Fact 3 gives the 1950 and 2017 averages and supports a major decline. The other choices keep the common error that family size barely changed.

questions.prompt: Two briefings explain falling fertility. One names only contraception; one names several linked conditions. Which briefing fits the source?
choices: Fertility falls as child survival, education, rights, poverty, and contraception reinforce each other.
Fertility falls when contraception appears, while other social changes are side details.
Fertility falls when families copy rich countries, regardless of survival or education.
questions.explanation: Fact 4 names several determinants working together. The common error is turning a fertility transition into a one-cause story about contraception alone.

questions.prompt: A report shows a short recent segment of a curve that looks straight. What should the editor check before extending it?
choices: Whether the straight segment has the cleanest visual design for readers.
Whether a wider window reveals a bend hidden by the tight crop.
Whether the recent slope is steep enough to make the forecast memorable.
questions.explanation: Fact 5 says a small part of a curve can look straight. The first check is the viewing window, not the neatness or drama of the recent segment.

questions.prompt: A designer laying out the page tests the straight line instinct with this prompt. A development dashboard treats every indicator as a straight rise with income. Which correction fits the source?
choices: Different mechanisms can make lines rise, flatten, slide, or hump.
Income removes the need to inspect the shape of each indicator.
Straight lines are safest when the chart covers many countries.
questions.explanation: Fact 6 supports a gallery of shapes. Saturation, thresholds, and behavior change can bend a line, so income alone does not make every indicator straight.

questions.prompt: A writer polishing a paragraph uses the straight line instinct to choose. The colleague says population forecasts are just guesses. Which reply fits the source note about UN forecasts?
choices: Forecasts should be ignored unless they predict the exact population far ahead.
Forecasts can be checked against later outcomes and have a track record.
Forecasts are useful only when they avoid age structure and fertility assumptions.
questions.explanation: Fact 7 says UN forecasts have a measurable record. That does not make them perfect, but it does make them more than unchecked guesses.

questions.prompt: The forecast writer hears that two children per woman is always replacement everywhere. Which answer matches the source note?
choices: Two children is exact replacement in the forecast writer's note because each pair has two parents.
Replacement can be around 2.3 globally because mortality changes the threshold.
Replacement rises only when families prefer larger households for cultural reasons.
questions.explanation: Fact 8 says replacement depends on mortality conditions and cites about 2.3 globally. The simple two-parent arithmetic misses deaths before replacement can happen.

questions.prompt: A chart has climbed for five years, and the newsletter editor wants to extend the current slope. What should happen before he trusts that forecast?
choices: He should extend the line first, then look for causes after the forecast is drawn.
He should prefer the current slope because the latest five years are the clearest clue.
He should ask which mechanism could keep the slope straight or bend it.
questions.explanation: Fact 9 gives the core repair: ask why the line might bend before extrapolating. A recent slope without a mechanism is only a drawing habit.

reviewCards.front: What is the straight line instinct asking the reader to distrust?
reviewCards.back: Distrust the reflex that a recent slope will keep the same speed and direction. The repair is to ask what kind of line this could be and what cause could bend it.

reviewCards.front: Why does total population growth not automatically mean more children through 2100?
reviewCards.back: The UN WPP 2017 medium variant puts the 2100 child count close to the 2017 count after a mid-century peak. Much projected growth comes from adults and older people.

reviewCards.front: Why is contraception alone too thin an explanation for falling fertility?
reviewCards.back: Fertility transitions usually need several conditions at once: child survival, education, women's rights, lower poverty, and contraception. The bend comes from the mix.

reviewCards.front: What does Jordan Ellenberg's circle lesson warn you about when reading a chart?
reviewCards.back: A tiny part of a curve can look straight. Before extending a recent segment, widen the view and ask whether the crop is hiding the line's real shape.

reviewCards.front: What does Trend Check (Ch 2) get WRONG if applied naively to the population forecast case?
reviewCards.back: Trend Check can tell level and direction, but it can still tempt a straight extension. Bend Check adds the cause question: what would keep the slope straight, and what could bend it?

implementationPlan.title: Ask Why Lines Bend
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice Bend Check before you accept a rising or falling line. Name the visible slope, widen the window, then ask what force could bend it. The skill is not doubt for its own sake; it is asking the cause to earn the forecast.

ifThenPlans.context: When population growth makes someone picture endless children
ifThenPlans.plan: If a population claim sounds like more babies forever, then check the child count and the age structure before repeating it.

ifThenPlans.context: When a short fertility chart looks calm
ifThenPlans.plan: If a recent slice makes family size look fixed, then widen the dates until the 1950 to 2017 bend is visible.

ifThenPlans.context: When a cropped chart looks straight
ifThenPlans.plan: If the crop makes the slope feel certain, then ask for the wider view before drawing the next segment.

ifThenPlans.context: When a forecast feels obvious
ifThenPlans.plan: If the next step looks like a ruler line, then name the mechanism that would keep it straight or bend it.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Set a question mark beside the number in any trend claim you meet, then name three forces that could bend the line before you answer.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: For one week, swap your first forecast habit. In the first half, notice when you extend the latest slope. In the second half, replace that habit with Bend Check and compare which half gave better questions.

memorableLines.text: Do not extend a line until you can name its cause.
memorableLines.why: It turns forecasting into a demand for a cause.

memorableLines.text: A short window can hide a curve.
memorableLines.why: It makes the scale problem easy to remember.

memorableLines.text: Population growth can come from age structure, not more children.
memorableLines.why: It gives readers a portable warning before they extrapolate.

chapters.title: The Fear Instinct
chapters.hook: The body jumps at a siren, but the quiet risk table may deserve the next dollar.
chapters.counterintuition: Fear can save you and mislead you. It wakes the body before the numbers arrive, so the next step is to compare danger, exposure, probability, and scale.
chapters.tryThisNow: When a frightening claim lands today, write this above your answer: what is the risk after I check exposure, probability, and scale?
chapters.keyTakeaway: Treat fear as an alarm, then check danger, exposure, probability, and scale before you decide what deserves attention, money, or a reply.

breakdown.fastRead:
The reader runs a finger down two poll lists: Gallup in the United States and YouGov in the United Kingdom. Snakes, heights, and public speaking sit near the top. None of those lists is a death table.

The fear instinct makes vivid dangers feel large. It reacts fast to fangs, cliffs, crowds, crashes, radiation, and terror. That speed can help when a snake is near your boot. Fear is an alarm, not a scale.

Use a Risk Check before you rank a danger. Ask what can hurt, how many people meet it, how likely harm is, and how large the harm is beside other risks.
breakdown.deepRead:
A poll list can make a snake feel larger than a hospital ward. The body sees an image and sends attention there first. Then the mind starts shopping for proof. A plane crash, a terror attack, or a radiation leak feels like a full answer because it is easy to picture.

EM-DAT, the international disaster database, gives a calmer comparison. The old ten-year average was 325,742 annual disaster deaths in 1907-1916. The later average was 80,386 in 2007-2016. The room may expect a story about growing danger. The table says deaths fell by about three quarters.

The per-person line cuts harder. Disaster deaths fell from 181 per million people to 11 per million in the same comparison. More people lived on Earth, but warning systems, stronger buildings, relief work, and planning changed the odds. A scary story can be true and still be small.

This does not make floods, quakes, or storms harmless. It changes the first question. Do not ask only, "Am I scared?" Ask, "What is the measured risk, and what else could use the same money or attention?" Risk Check means asking what can hurt, how many people meet it, how likely harm is, and how large the harm is. It lets fear keep its useful job. It can point to danger without getting to run the budget.
breakdown.fullRead:
Write Fukushima at the top of a briefing page, then stop before the next word. The loudest image is the nuclear plant. The larger event was Japan's 2011 Tohoku earthquake and tsunami, not only the damaged plant.

That pause matters because one feared agent can swallow a whole pathway. Official sources cited in the notes reported no confirmed direct deaths from the nuclear leak itself. The evacuation still hurt frail patients. The fear was not fake. The label was too narrow.

Count the pathway before you name the villain. An earthquake shakes the coast. A tsunami kills. An evacuation moves frail patients. A nuclear leak creates dread and hard public-health questions. If all of that becomes only "radiation danger," then money and rules may chase the image instead of the main route of harm.

The same habit works on air travel. A crash makes the news because it is rare, sudden, and visual. A useful safety claim needs passenger exposure, flight volume, and passenger miles. Without exposure, a death count floats in the air. It cannot tell you whether flying is more dangerous than the trip you took to the airport.

Terrorism pushes the fear instinct even harder because intent feels personal. A planned attack seems to reach through the screen. That is why it can receive more attention than larger familiar risks. Newsworthiness and death risk are different measures. One asks what people will watch. The other asks how many people are harmed.

A fear list has the same trap in softer clothes. Snakes and heights belong on a survey because they are easy for the body to picture. Public speaking belongs there because a room full of faces can feel like danger. But a list of fears is not a triage board. It tells you where the alarm is loud, not where the next life can be saved.

Uncertainty does not end the work. War deaths are hard to count, and methods disagree. That does not mean comparison is useless. It means the range should be wide, the source should be named, and the conclusion should stay modest. When the data are blurry, do not pretend to see sharply. Do not shut your eyes either.

The boundary is fit. A driver who feels the tires break loose on ice does not pull up a chart of regional crash rates before easing off the wheel. The Risk Check helps before ranking risks, writing policy, spending money, or replying to a frightening claim. It belongs after the correction, when there is time to rank the next risk.

examples.title: Fear Lists Are Not Death Tables
examples.scenario: At 8:18 a.m., an analyst in the Fukushima briefing room marks risk table 4-1; Gallup and YouGov fear lists put snakes, heights, and public speaking near the top. Those lists show what people fear, not what kills most people.
examples.whatToDo: Write feared is not the same as frequent, then add a separate risk column.
examples.whyItMatters: The quiet margin teaches the first split. When a reader sees a ranked fear list, the next move is to ask what the list measures before treating it as danger.

examples.title: The EM-DAT Disaster Comparison
examples.scenario: At 8:19 a.m., an analyst in the Fukushima briefing room marks risk table 4-2; EM-DAT gives an old ten-year average of 325,742 annual disaster deaths for 1907-1916 and 80,386 for 2007-2016. Per million people, the comparison falls from 181 to 11.
examples.whatToDo: Keep raw counts and per-person rates together.
examples.whyItMatters: The exchange slows the scary headline. A reader learns to compare time spans and exposure before assuming that more news means more danger.

examples.title: Fukushima, Tsunami, Evacuation
examples.scenario: At 8:20 a.m., an analyst in the Fukushima briefing room marks risk table 4-3; The 2011 event was the Tohoku earthquake and tsunami, with official sources cited in the notes reporting no confirmed direct deaths from the nuclear leak itself. Evacuation still harmed frail patients.
examples.whatToDo: Separate the pathway before naming the feared agent.
examples.whyItMatters: The repair protects the mechanism. Readers learn to separate the feared agent from the full chain of harm before they plan or judge a response.

examples.title: The Four Risk Questions
examples.scenario: At 8:21 a.m., an analyst in the Fukushima briefing room marks risk table 4-4; A careful reply asks what can hurt, how many people are exposed, how likely harm is, and how large that harm is beside other risks.
examples.whatToDo: Write the risk question before answering the frightening claim.
examples.whyItMatters: The memo turns risk work into a usable pause. The reader gets words to place between fear and the next message, not just an idea to admire.

examples.title: Storm Clips and Disaster Rates
examples.scenario: At 8:22 a.m., an analyst in the Fukushima briefing room marks risk table 4-5; Storm footage can deserve attention without setting the whole budget. EM-DAT rates and exposure help decide what belongs first.
examples.whatToDo: Use clips as evidence of fear; use rates to rank the agenda.
examples.whyItMatters: The contrast shows how attention gets spent. Vivid footage may deserve action, but it should not outrank measures that reduce the larger or more likely harm.

examples.title: Intent and Arithmetic
examples.scenario: At 8:23 a.m., an analyst in the Fukushima briefing room marks risk table 4-6; Terrorism feels especially frightening because intent is part of the harm. The broadcast still needs deaths and exposure before it uses airtime as a risk score.
examples.whatToDo: Keep the item serious while adding larger familiar risks for scale.
examples.whyItMatters: The coach line gives the reader a portable check. Media attention can signal salience, but it cannot stand in for measured harm.

questions.prompt: A Gallup list puts snakes, heights, and public speaking near the top of reported fears. What should the reader conclude before calling them the biggest dangers?
choices: The list ranks what feels vivid, not what kills the most people.
The list ranks rare fears that people mention only when prompted.
The list ranks modern dangers that death records often miss.
questions.explanation: Fact 1 separates reported fear from mortality risk. Snakes, heights, and public speaking can rank high in fear without ranking high as causes of death.

questions.prompt: An EM-DAT table shows about 325,742 annual disaster deaths in 1907-1916 and about 80,386 in 2007-2016. Which reading fits the data?
choices: Annual disaster deaths stayed high because the later count still contains tens of thousands.
Annual disaster deaths rose in hidden ways because the world population grew.
Annual disaster deaths fell by about three quarters in the ten-year averages.
questions.explanation: Fact 2 supports the large raw decline. The later count is still tragic, but it is far lower than the early-century average.

questions.prompt: The same disaster comparison drops from 181 deaths per million people to 11 per million. What does that add beyond the raw count?
choices: It shows that raw counts are enough when the same database is used.
It shows that a larger population makes every disaster trend less useful.
It shows that exposure changed, so per-person risk fell even more sharply.
questions.explanation: Fact 3 says per-capita risk fell even more. The raw count matters, but deaths per million adjusts for the larger exposed population.

questions.prompt: The briefer is drafting a public note after Japan's 2011 disaster and starts to call Fukushima a case of nuclear leak deaths. Which correction matches the source notes?
choices: The documented harm centered on the earthquake, tsunami, and evacuation pathway, not confirmed direct leak deaths.
The documented harm centered on radiation mortality that later records made hard to separate.
The documented harm centered on public fear, while the tsunami and evacuation were secondary.
questions.explanation: Fact 4 names the earthquake, tsunami, and evacuation harms. The cited official accounts reported no confirmed direct deaths from the leak itself.

questions.prompt: A few plane crashes make flying feel newly dangerous. Which comparison should the clinic manager ask for before judging flight safety?
choices: Compare the crash stories with the number of news reports that used them.
Compare fatalities with passenger miles and total flight volume.
Compare the newest crash with the most familiar road accident.
questions.explanation: Fact 6 requires exposure. Fatalities mean little for safety judgment unless they are compared with passenger miles and flight volume.

questions.prompt: Two news editors see the same terrorist attack. One treats airtime as the risk measure; the other asks for deaths beside familiar risks. Which response fits the fear lesson?
choices: The second response fits because drama and intent can make rare events seem larger than their death risk.
The first response fits because airtime usually follows the risks that harm the most people.
The first response fits because planned violence should be counted apart from ordinary death causes.
questions.explanation: Fact 8 separates media attention from death risk. Terrorism can be salient because intent and drama are newsworthy, not because airtime measures mortality burden.

questions.prompt: A frightening voicemail makes the data lead want to redirect the whole budget. Which first check follows the fear instinct correction?
choices: He should ask whether the caller sounded calm, exposed, and certain.
He should ask whether the danger feels vivid enough to keep attention.
He should ask about danger, exposure, probability, and scale before ranking it.
questions.explanation: Fact 9 says risk combines danger, exposure, and probability rather than emotional intensity. Scale decides whether it deserves scarce resources.

questions.prompt: A contamination scare spreads before the measured health review is finished. Which harm should the broadcaster keep in the risk picture?
choices: Measured harm can include only confirmed radiation deaths after exposure records close.
Measured harm can include anxiety, stress, and evacuation damage as well as radiation questions.
Measured harm can include public dread only when direct deaths are already confirmed.
questions.explanation: Fact 7 keeps psychosocial effects and evacuation damage in view. The source does not limit harm to confirmed radiation deaths.

questions.prompt: The clinic manager is comparing war death estimates before replying to a worried colleague, and two methods disagree. Which answer uses uncertainty the way the Risk Check advises?
choices: Drop the comparison until one method produces a single clean count.
Keep wider ranges and compare cautiously instead of refusing all comparison.
Choose the lower estimate when the higher estimate might cause fear.
questions.explanation: Fact 5 says uncertainty should widen ranges, not end comparison. A cautious range is better than pretending the data are useless or clean.

reviewCards.front: What does the fear instinct make your attention do first?
reviewCards.back: It sends attention toward vivid danger before you have compared exposure, probability, and scale. The alarm may be useful, but it is not yet a risk ranking.

reviewCards.front: Why are the Gallup and YouGov fear polls not a danger ranking?
reviewCards.back: They measure reported fear. Snakes, heights, and public speaking can feel large in the mind without being the hazards that kill the most people.

reviewCards.front: Recall the straight line instinct (Ch 3): name one concrete moment here where it actually bites.
reviewCards.back: The EM-DAT disaster line bites here. A reader may expect more people to mean rising disaster deaths, but the per-million rate falls from 181 to 11.

reviewCards.front: What should the Fukushima case make you separate?
reviewCards.back: Separate the feared agent from the event pathway. The notes cite earthquake, tsunami, and evacuation harms while reporting no confirmed direct deaths from the leak itself.

reviewCards.front: What four checks belong in a Risk Check?
reviewCards.back: Ask what can hurt, how many people are exposed, how likely harm is, and how large the harm is beside other risks competing for the same attention.

reviewCards.front: Why can terrorism draw more attention than larger familiar risks?
reviewCards.back: Intent and drama make rare events easy to picture and report. Media salience can be high even when the mortality burden is lower than familiar risks.

implementationPlan.title: Check Risk Before Replying
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice a Risk Check before you answer a frightening claim. Write the actual words that ask for danger, exposure, probability, and scale. The skill is not calmness for show; it is giving the numbers a turn before fear sets the order.

ifThenPlans.context: When a fear list or poll gets treated as a danger list
ifThenPlans.plan: If a ranked fear list appears in a reply thread, then write: "This ranks fear; what death or exposure data would rank risk?"

ifThenPlans.context: When a disaster headline makes the world feel less safe
ifThenPlans.plan: If the headline makes danger feel obvious, then ask for both raw deaths and deaths per million before you answer.

ifThenPlans.context: When one feared agent gets blamed for a whole event
ifThenPlans.plan: If the reply names one villain too fast, then write the full harm pathway before you agree or object.

ifThenPlans.context: When airtime feels like proof of priority
ifThenPlans.plan: If the story is everywhere, then ask whether news attention is measuring deaths, exposure, or only salience.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Draft the sentence now, while you are calm ("What are the danger, exposure, probability, and scale?"), so the next frightening claim meets a question, not a reflex.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: This week, teach Risk Check to one other person in your own words. Use the Gallup, EM-DAT, or Fukushima case, then ask them to explain it back.

memorableLines.text: Fear is an alarm, not a risk table.
memorableLines.why: It makes the core distinction short enough to use under pressure.

memorableLines.text: A vivid danger can be real and still not be the largest risk.
memorableLines.why: It prevents readers from confusing truth with size.

memorableLines.text: Count the pathway before naming the feared agent.
memorableLines.why: It captures the Fukushima lesson without losing the action step.

chapters.title: The Size Instinct
chapters.hook: Two UK guesses ran about 1.9x and 2.6x high because visible groups felt larger than measured shares.
chapters.counterintuition: A big number is not yet a big share. A denominator, the whole you divide by, tells you what the number is large compared with.
chapters.tryThisNow: For the next 10 minutes, when a big number tempts you, write the missing denominator beside it before repeating it.
chapters.keyTakeaway: A big number earns trust only after you divide it by the right whole, compare it with a fair alternative, and rank what the next dollar can change.

breakdown.fastRead:
The planner sees the same hospital ledger in Nacala, Mozambique, twice. The first look hurts: child deaths on a page. The later look adds births, population, and hospital records, then turns the count into a rate. Now the question changes from how awful this number feels to where a scarce doctor can save the most children.

The size instinct is the reflex to treat a large number as meaning all by itself. It does not. Big numbers need a place to stand. Use Add the Missing Denominator: ask what total, trend, or alternative would make this number useful.
breakdown.deepRead:
A number grabs attention before it explains itself. That is why the Nacala case matters. Mozambique was the poorest country in 1979, and the source notes show extremely few doctors per 100,000 people around 1980. In that setting, one wrong priority can cost many lives.

The repair starts with a plain check: choose the denominator that fits the decision. If the choice is about child mortality, divide deaths by births or by children exposed. If it is about public-health money, compare lives saved per dollar. If it is about a social share, compare a guess with the measured share of the whole.

This matters in a UNICEF budget discussion. Advanced care can sound like the strongest medicine, but the poorest children may need low-cost high-impact interventions first. The mistake is ranking by drama instead of lives saved per cost.

That correction does not insult advanced care. It only puts first dollars where they do the most work. Drama is not the same as size, and size is not the same as priority. A shiny treatment can be real and still be the wrong first use of a small public-health budget.
breakdown.fullRead:
The Ipsos MORI Perils of Perception 2015 figures are useful because no one in the room has to be lying. UK respondents guessed the immigrant share at 25 percent, while the measured share was 13 percent. Wealth got stretched too: they guessed 59 percent for the top 1 percent share, not the measured 23 percent.

The mistake is easy to understand. People do not carry census tables in their heads. They carry stories, streets, headlines, and faces. If a group is visible in the mind, the mind can count it too high. The denominator habit slows that jump. It asks, compared with what whole?

The same move works for infant deaths. A death total can make the room silent and still leave out the risk per baby. If births rose while the death rate fell, the raw number can hide real progress. The humane response is not to numb yourself. It is to ask two questions at once: how many families were harmed, and what happened to risk per child over time?

A headline about war deaths is harder. A remembered war number is emotionally large. It still needs population, period, and a fair comparison before it can set today's priority. Memory and scale are cousins, not twins.

The same habit applies to stories about bears and domestic violence. Bear attacks are dramatic. Repeated intimate-partner killings are less cinematic and far more common in the source comparison. A policy agenda that follows shock alone can walk past preventable harm.

The hard edge is that not every denominator helps. A hospital death count divided by the number of hospital beds may look precise while answering the wrong question. If the decision is where to send health workers, births and population matter more. If the decision is how to spend a public-health dollar, cost per life saved matters more. Divide only by what the choice needs.

That is why the question is not arithmetic in general. It is what the next action needs to know. A district note about Nacala should not use the same comparison as a donor note about UNICEF. One is asking where children are dying relative to births and population. The other is asking which public-health option saves the most lives with the next dollar. Both use proportion. They do not use the same proportion.

This also keeps the idea from becoming cold. A denominator is not a way to make suffering look smaller. It is a way to stop one visible suffering from stealing all the help. When the page shows child deaths, the first duty is to care. The next duty is to count well enough that care reaches the children most likely to die next.

Here is the counter-case. If the task is checking whether the UK poll guess itself was recorded correctly, do not divide first. Compare the transcript, sample note, and published figure. Proportion helps judgment after the number is real. It should not replace the basic check that the number was copied correctly.

examples.title: Nacala Needs the Right Whole
examples.scenario: At 8:24 a.m., a health planner in the Nacala clinic office marks budget sheet 5-1; A Nacala hospital ledger of child deaths is not enough to allocate scarce doctors. The count needs births, district population, and child-mortality rates.
examples.whatToDo: Add the right denominator before writing the priority note.
examples.whyItMatters: The same page can point to different action after the denominator arrives. A reader learns to respect the grief in the count without letting the count choose alone.

examples.title: UNICEF Cost per Life Saved
examples.scenario: At 8:25 a.m., a health planner in the Nacala clinic office marks budget sheet 5-2; In a UNICEF budget discussion, prestige medicine can sound strongest while low-cost interventions save more lives per dollar among the poorest children.
examples.whatToDo: Rank options by cost per life saved, not by how impressive the equipment sounds.
examples.whyItMatters: The useful moment is the catch. Readers need to notice when a dramatic option has stolen the ranking that a scarce budget should decide.

examples.title: Ipsos MORI Misperceptions
examples.scenario: At 8:26 a.m., a health planner in the Nacala clinic office marks budget sheet 5-3; In the UK figures from Ipsos MORI Perils of Perception 2015, respondents guessed immigrants at 25% when the measured share was 13%, and guessed the top 1% wealth share at 59% when the measured share was 23%.
examples.whatToDo: Put guessed share beside measured share and ask what whole is missing.
examples.whyItMatters: The table turns a scolding impulse into a proportion check. Readers can see how a mind inflates what it notices often.

examples.title: Deaths and Death Rates
examples.scenario: At 8:27 a.m., a health planner in the Nacala clinic office marks budget sheet 5-4; A raw infant-death total carries grief. Deaths per birth over time carries the risk trend. A humane chart can show both without confusing them.
examples.whatToDo: Give the main chart to the rate and keep the raw total in the caption.
examples.whyItMatters: A plan can honor grief and still show direction. The reader learns that progress is visible only when the count meets births and past years.

examples.title: The Wrong Denominator
examples.scenario: At 8:28 a.m., a health planner in the Nacala clinic office marks budget sheet 5-5; Dividing deaths by hospital beds can look careful while answering the wrong allocation question. Births and population fit the decision better.
examples.whatToDo: Reject both the vivid raw count and the tidy wrong proportion.
examples.whyItMatters: The scene protects the hard edge. Division helps only when the denominator fits the decision.

examples.title: Bears and Domestic Violence
examples.scenario: At 8:29 a.m., a health planner in the Nacala clinic office marks budget sheet 5-6; A bear attack story is dramatic, but repeated intimate-partner killings are far more common in the source comparison. Attention can drift away from preventable harm.
examples.whatToDo: Use the dramatic case only to show why the agenda needs scale.
examples.whyItMatters: The exchange ranks harm instead of shock. Readers can use the same move when a rare event takes over the agenda.

questions.prompt: The planner sees child deaths in the Nacala hospital ledger while doctors are scarce. Which first step makes the number useful for action?
choices: He combines deaths with births, population, and records to make a child mortality rate.
He treats the hospital death count as the clearest guide for where doctors should go.
He waits for a later census before making any comparison from the hospital records.
questions.explanation: Fact 1 says the Nacala deaths needed births, population, and hospital records before they could guide action. The raw count alone can misdirect scarce help.

questions.prompt: Two UNICEF proposals aim to help the poorest children. One ranks advanced care first; one ranks basic measures by lives saved per dollar. Which fits the source?
choices: Advanced care should lead because the strongest treatment is the safest first use of funds.
Basic measures should wait until every advanced option has been checked for possible reach.
Low-cost high-impact measures can lead when limited budgets make cost per life saved decisive.
questions.explanation: Fact 3 supports ranking by lives saved per dollar in poor settings. Advanced care may matter, but it is not always the best first use of scarce funds.

questions.prompt: An Ipsos MORI table shows UK guesses far above measured figures for immigration and top-1-percent wealth. What reading follows?
choices: Public guesses about visible groups usually track official shares closely enough for debate.
Visible examples can inflate mental counts far beyond measured shares of the whole.
Poll errors mainly prove that respondents confuse wealth figures with immigration figures.
questions.explanation: Fact 4 says people overestimate visible proportions. The UK guesses of 25 versus 13 percent and 59 versus 23 percent show salience inflating shares.

questions.prompt: The district planner divides a health number before moving health workers, then still feels unsure. Which warning best matches the hard edge?
choices: Any proportion is safer than a raw number because division removes emotional bias.
A proportion helps only when its denominator matches the choice being made.
A denominator should be chosen for speed so the decision does not stall.
questions.explanation: Fact 8 says the denominator must fit the decision: per birth, per dollar, per population, or per exposure. A bad denominator can mislead too.

questions.prompt: The health analyst has one chart slot before a clinic briefing where parents will hear about infant deaths. Which data view should carry the main chart?
choices: The raw death total alone, since any large infant death number proves that progress has stopped.
The latest year's death count alone, since the most recent total is the most relevant signal.
