examples.whyItMatters: The reveal breaks a common shortcut. A topic can be urgent while some of its best official numbers still arrive slowly.

examples.title: Repetition Is Not Verification
examples.scenario: At 8:58 a.m., a policy analyst in the Foresight cabinet office marks source note 10-5; A number repeated everywhere may still come from one or two original sources. UNHCR and other source checks belong before the number travels again.
examples.whatToDo: Add the source-chain line before sharing the figure.
examples.whyItMatters: The thread shows how to slow one number without dismissing the people at risk. Repeated estimates still need a first-source check.

examples.title: Route, Freshness, Side Effect
examples.scenario: At 8:59 a.m., a policy analyst in the Foresight cabinet office marks source note 10-6; An all-caps crisis link says there is no time. The smallest useful pause asks how the danger travels, how fresh the evidence is, and what side effect the action may cause.
examples.whatToDo: Put the phone down long enough to check the first source.
examples.whyItMatters: The pause is not delay for its own sake. It turns urgent energy into a smaller action that can still learn.

questions.prompt: The responder sees a strict Ebola roadblock on the main road, but the contact map shows river and forest movement. Which reading fits the urgency rule?
choices: The roadblock should be judged by how visible and orderly it looks to worried people.
The roadblock should be tested against routes contacts can still use to move.
The roadblock should be replaced by a slower review before any field action starts.
questions.explanation: Fact 1 says controls can fail when contacts move by canoe or forest path. Visibility is not enough, and the answer is not slow review; it is checking the route.

questions.prompt: The policy analyst hears a policy call turn into two options: publish the scariest number or ignore the issue. What should she challenge?
choices: She should challenge the either-or frame and keep room for ranges, checks, and options.
She should challenge the slowest speaker and push the group toward a single public line.
She should challenge the topic itself until the group can prove there is no uncertainty.
questions.explanation: Fact 2 warns that urgency creates false binaries. The policy analyst should keep ranges and options alive, not force one line or treat uncertainty as denial.

questions.prompt: The analyst is writing a public caption for a fresh-looking climate image and an older OECD emissions table. The packet looks current. Which check comes first?
choices: He should treat the official tables as current because the climate image updated today.
He should delay the whole packet until every indicator can share one reporting date.
He should mark each indicator's own publication lag before claiming precision.
questions.explanation: Fact 5 says data freshness differs by indicator. GDP and CO2 can have very different lags, so the analyst needs dates per measure, not one shared clock.

questions.prompt: The junior analyst sees the same climate-migration estimate quoted in many reports. What is the first inference Foresight 2011 supports?
choices: The repeated number has become reliable enough because many writers now cite it.
The repeated number may still trace back to a thin chain of original sources.
The repeated number should be ignored until migration stops changing across regions.
questions.explanation: Fact 4 says repetition can amplify weak original estimates. The issue is source-chain strength, not the number's fame or a reason to ignore migration.

questions.prompt: The colleague is editing a climate handout and removes one single apocalypse story. A colleague says that sounds like denial. Which response best fits the evidence?
choices: He should accept the single story because severe risks need one clear public scenario.
He should narrow the climate topic because complex causes make public action less clear.
He should say climate is severe even when no one scenario explains the whole future.
questions.explanation: Fact 3 separates serious climate risk from one simple event. Rejecting a single catastrophe frame is not denial; it protects a complex risk from a bad story.

questions.prompt: The reviewer is sorting risks for a public talk and moves pandemics below daily worries because he thinks factfulness means less alarm. How should the risk list correct him?
choices: Pandemic risk belongs on the short list with financial collapse, world war, climate-resource risk, and extreme poverty.
Pandemic risk belongs below daily worries because broad progress makes rare events less useful to study.
Pandemic risk belongs outside the method because outbreak fear can distort every other fact check.
questions.explanation: Fact 6 places global pandemic on the short risk list. Factfulness narrows attention to major risks; it does not erase pandemic concern.

questions.prompt: The caller hears a call to restrict antibiotics everywhere as the safest response. Which answer best fits disciplined speed?
choices: He should back the broad restriction because overuse is the only antibiotic danger in view.
He should ask for a plan that cuts overuse while keeping cheap lifesaving access where needed.
He should avoid the issue because resistance and access point in opposite directions.
questions.explanation: Fact 7 says overuse is dangerous, but underaccess can also kill. Careful action must see both harms instead of turning panic into a blanket rule.

questions.prompt: The policy analyst sees a falling extreme-poverty rate and wants to move the issue off the urgent list. What should she notice?
choices: The remaining cases can be harder because many people are children, small-scale farmers, minorities, or near conflict.
The falling rate proves the remaining cases will keep falling if no one changes the current plan.
The rate matters less than the headline because urgency should focus on whatever scares people most.
questions.explanation: Fact 8 says extreme poverty remains an ongoing risk. A falling rate does not erase the harder remaining cases or justify headline-driven attention.

questions.prompt: A crisis link arrives while the junior analyst is in a group chat, and the sender says delay is dangerous. Which response uses disciplined speed?
choices: He should share first, then check later, because urgent action loses value if verification slows it.
He should wait for a perfect report, because small checks cannot protect people from urgent claims.
He should take one small step that checks the route, freshness, or side effect before he spreads it.
questions.explanation: Fact 9 supports disciplined speed: small checks keep facts in the loop. It rejects both blind sharing and waiting for perfect certainty.

reviewCards.front: How does the urgency instinct change a hard problem in your mind?
reviewCards.back: It makes a complex risk feel like a now-or-never choice. That pressure can stop data checks, hide side effects, and make visible action look better than aimed action.

reviewCards.front: Why did the Ebola roadblock warning matter in Kikwit 1995?
reviewCards.back: David L. Heymann's warning showed that a cordon can look forceful while contacts move through other routes, such as Kwilu River dugout canoes or forest paths.

reviewCards.front: What does the OECD lag case teach about fresh-looking data?
reviewCards.back: A climate image can look current while related official figures lag. The OECD December 2017 example pairs GDP figures weeks old, CO2 two years behind.

reviewCards.front: What should you check when a climate-migration number appears everywhere?
reviewCards.back: Check the first source chain and the adaptation assumptions. Dramatic climate-migration estimates can rest on thin source chains.

reviewCards.front: What are the three checks in Check the Urgent Route?
reviewCards.back: Name the path the risk uses, ask how current the evidence is, and choose a small step that can be corrected after the next fact arrives.

reviewCards.front: What does the generalization instinct (Ch 6) get WRONG if you applied it naively to the Ebola roadblocks case?
reviewCards.back: It might treat roadblocks as one category and assume the label predicts success. This case needs route checks: road, river, and forest paths behave differently.

implementationPlan.title: Check the Urgent Route
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice turning pressure into a route check. Name the path the danger uses, the age of the evidence, and one side effect of your first response. The skill lets you move quickly without letting urgency erase thought.

ifThenPlans.context: When a visible fix feels like proof of action
ifThenPlans.plan: If the visible fix calms the room, then Check the Urgent Route by asking which path the risk can still use.

ifThenPlans.context: When a chart looks fresh because one part updated
ifThenPlans.plan: If one chart updates fast, then Check the Urgent Route by marking the date for each indicator before you cite it.

ifThenPlans.context: When a large number appears in many places
ifThenPlans.plan: If repetition makes a number feel settled, then Check the Urgent Route by tracing it to the first source you can find.

ifThenPlans.context: When pressure says there is no time to verify
ifThenPlans.plan: If urgency tells you to skip verification, then Check the Urgent Route by naming one small check you can do before the action spreads.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Urgency wants the wheel. The next claim that demands an instant reaction, jot route, freshness, and side effect first, then act on what they say.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: At the end of this week, look back once at the strongest urgent claim you met. Name what changed about your route check after you separated speed from panic.

memorableLines.text: Speed helps only after it is aimed.
memorableLines.why: It gives the urgency warning a short image without praising delay.

memorableLines.text: A visible barrier can hide a route around it.
memorableLines.why: It compresses the Ebola roadblock case into a useful test.

memorableLines.text: Serious risk deserves clean facts.
memorableLines.why: It captures the hard edge: concern and discipline belong together.

chapters.title: Factfulness in Practice
chapters.hook: Better facts do not stay useful unless people practice changing their minds.
chapters.counterintuition: The paradox is blunt: better facts can spread while old views survive, because tools matter only when people build a habit around them.
chapters.tryThisNow: When you draft your next factual reply, ask one person: which fact am I treating as settled here? Listen, then update one sentence.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Factfulness becomes useful when a person turns better data into a repeatable habit: ask one live question, count what appears, and update before the old story hardens.

breakdown.fastRead:
In a teacher chat for Gapminder Teach, the teacher has a free lesson open and 3 wrong student guesses circled in red. The easy plan is to correct the answers and move on. The better plan is to rehearse the move: show the guess, compare it with the data, and ask why the old picture felt so true.

Factfulness in practice means building that move into ordinary work. It is not a badge for people who know more facts. It is a routine that catches a stale picture before it steers a lesson, a story, a strategy, or a reply. A habit outlasts a headline.

The rule is small enough to use: ask where the claim came from, count what you can see, then update one next action. If the routine is missing, even good data becomes a poster on the wall.
breakdown.deepRead:
The habit works because it makes error visible before pride protects it. A person can defend an old world map for years if nobody asks them to make a guess first. Gapminder Teach makes the guess public in a low-stakes way. A class can see that its first answer was not stupidity. It was an old picture that had never been checked.

Business planning meets the same mechanism before a business plan is written. He starts with the old line: rich countries design, poorer countries make, and the West sells to the rest. Then he catches the mistake. Thomas L. Friedman 2005 helped people see services moving across borders. Fareed Zakaria 2008 pushed attention toward a post-American world. Bangladesh and Cambodia textiles make the shift concrete. Ghana, Nigeria, and Kenya belong in the plan as markets and investment settings, not as charity backdrops.

That correction changes the next question. The strategist no longer asks, "Where do we sell after the rich markets are full?" He asks which income levels are gaining skills, wages, and customers. Markets move when skills move.

The same pattern works for public facts. Tim Berners-Lee's linked-data vision makes checking less private. Gapminder bubble graphs let ordinary people inspect change instead of waiting for a gatekeeper to summarize it. Open data turns checking into citizenship.

The hard part is not admiring any one tool. It is choosing the next check while the old story still feels smooth. A teacher can do it before a lesson. A business planner does it before a market bet. A reader can do it before sending a reply.
breakdown.fullRead:
The worry before practice starts is fair: if everything must be checked, nothing will get done. Nobody can rebuild a worldview before every email. Factfulness in practice needs a small door, not a life-size research project.

The door is Ask, Count, Update. Ask one person a live question. Count one visible pattern. Update one sentence or one next step. The move is humble because it assumes the first answer may be wrong. It is practical because the work fits inside the moment before action.

Constructive journalism and local data displays show the public version of the same habit. A journalist can ask what context would make a bad event clearer: a base rate, a trend, or a local comparison. A local-data designer can start from the other end by asking which nearby fact people will guess wrong before reading. One begins with a story that needs context. One begins with a place that needs a number. Both refuse the lazy choice between bad news and happy news.

This matters because local ignorance is still ignorance. A person can know the global child mortality trend and still misread the street outside the school. Alan Smith's statistics talk points to the same lesson: the facts nearest to us may be the ones we check least.

Business has its own trap. A map that says West and Rest feels tidy. Thomas L. Friedman and Fareed Zakaria helped crack that map open, but the new habit must keep going. Bangladesh and Cambodia do not stay frozen as low-cost production sites. Rising incomes can move textile work toward newer lower-cost regions such as Kenya. Ghana, Nigeria, and Kenya can show up as commercial opportunities. The Atlas of Economic Complexity adds another check: look at existing skills and industries before guessing what a country can build next.

The open-data case adds the floor under all this. Public indicators, linked data, and Gapminder visuals make it harder for facts to stay locked inside expert rooms. They do not make every reader careful. They make care possible for more people.

The boundary is a person with a live duty and no room for a count. A paramedic treating a child at the curb needs hands free for care, not a worldview audit. The habit fits the planner, teacher, editor, analyst, and citizen before a claim travels. It belongs before the claim moves, not while someone needs hands-on care.

examples.title: Gapminder Teach First Guess
examples.scenario: At 9:00 a.m., a teacher in the Berners-Lee school office marks worksheet 11-1; Gapminder Teach works by making the first guess visible and low-stakes. The wrong answer is not a mess to hide; it is the old map becoming teachable.
examples.whatToDo: Write the first guess into the lesson plan before the data reveal.
examples.whyItMatters: The exchange turns factfulness into practice instead of trivia. A wrong guess becomes material the class can inspect, not a private failure to hide.

examples.title: From West-and-Rest to Moving Markets
examples.scenario: At 9:01 a.m., a teacher in the Berners-Lee school office marks worksheet 11-2; Thomas L. Friedman 2005, Fareed Zakaria 2008, Bangladesh and Cambodia textiles, and markets in Ghana, Nigeria, and Kenya all strain the old West-and-Rest map.
examples.whatToDo: Replace the arrow with skills, wages, income levels, and customers to check.
examples.whyItMatters: The recovery matters because the error arrived in a polished sentence. The useful habit catches the stale map while there is still time to change the plan.

examples.title: Public Data as a Check
examples.scenario: At 9:02 a.m., a teacher in the Berners-Lee school office marks worksheet 11-3; Tim Berners-Lee's linked-data vision and Gapminder bubble graphs matter because readers can follow public indicators instead of trusting a summary alone.
examples.whatToDo: Keep chart and source path together.
examples.whyItMatters: The memo shows why open data is infrastructure for clear thinking. A reader who can inspect the source can correct the explainer too.

examples.title: Constructive Journalism and Local Data
examples.scenario: At 9:03 a.m., a teacher in the Berners-Lee school office marks worksheet 11-4; A hard local story needs context; a local data display needs a guessed number before the reveal. Both make the hidden assumption testable.
examples.whatToDo: Add a trend, base rate, or local comparison before publication.
examples.whyItMatters: The contrast keeps factfulness close to home. People can misread their own city as easily as they misread the world.

examples.title: Atlas of Economic Complexity
examples.scenario: At 9:04 a.m., a teacher in the Berners-Lee school office marks worksheet 11-5; The Atlas of Economic Complexity asks what skills and industries already exist before naming a bold next sector. Ambition is not a map.
examples.whatToDo: Mark nearby capabilities before choosing the next bet.
examples.whyItMatters: The coach talk makes diversification less like wishful ranking. A next industry is easier to study when the current skill base is on the table.

examples.title: Keep the First-Guess Column
examples.scenario: At 9:05 a.m., a teacher in the Berners-Lee school office marks worksheet 11-6; Removing the first-guess column can make the worksheet cleaner and the learning weaker. The visible old answer gives the class a safer way to change its mind.
examples.whatToDo: Leave the column and plan the comparison.
examples.whyItMatters: The school case protects the learning moment. If the wrong guess disappears, the class may get the answer without practicing the update.

questions.prompt: Two teachers prepare a Gapminder Teach lesson. The teacher begins with student guesses; the new teacher wants to reveal the chart first. Which plan fits the practice claim?
choices: The new teacher should reveal the chart first so students meet the right answer cleanly.
The teacher should use the guesses so students can practice correcting a misconception.
The new teacher should assign the reading once so the worldview update happens privately.
questions.explanation: Fact 1 points to reusable Gapminder materials and a teacher community. The practice is repeated correction, not one clean reveal or one private reading.

questions.prompt: The strategist's draft treats global business as rich countries selling to the rest. Which revision follows the Friedman and Zakaria source thread?
choices: He should keep the West-to-Rest frame but add more export examples from poorer regions.
He should focus on rich-country demand first and treat lower levels as future buyers.
He should track skills, wages, and consumers as industries move across income levels.
questions.explanation: Fact 2 says services and industries shift across income levels. The stale move is West selling to Rest, even when it adds more examples.

questions.prompt: A sourcing note lists Bangladesh and Cambodia textiles and assumes low-cost production will stay there. Which reading should change the plan?
choices: Those examples prove textile locations remain stable once a country builds the sector.
Those examples show that newer regions should wait until all rich markets are full.
Those examples show supply chains can move again as incomes and wages change.
questions.explanation: Fact 3 says development changes supply chains. The error is treating a low-income production location as fixed after it appears on the map.

questions.prompt: A student comparing two notes tries factfulness in practice here. A briefing shows Ghana, Nigeria, and Kenya only in an aid section. Which edit best matches the business lens here?
choices: Move them into the market scan as serious commercial opportunities to study.
Keep them in the aid section but add a note that growth may arrive later.
Remove them from the briefing until the investment case is already settled.
questions.explanation: Fact 4 frames Ghana, Nigeria, and Kenya as investment opportunities. The aid-only frame is the common error, not the business lens.

questions.prompt: A development team wants a new industry because it sounds bold. The Atlas of Economic Complexity points elsewhere. What should they read from it?
choices: They should study current industries and skills before choosing the next capability.
They should rank national ambition first and use the Atlas after the target is chosen.
They should pause diversification until the Atlas names one best-fitting industry.
questions.explanation: Fact 5 says the Atlas maps existing industries and skills into plausible next capabilities. It guides choices; it does not bless ambition afterward.

questions.prompt: The journalist covers a bad local event and adds context about trend and scale. A reader says constructive journalism means happy news. Which reply fits?
choices: It means saving the hard facts for later so the public can handle the context first.
It means improving the information around bad events, not pretending they vanished.
It means replacing one frightening story with a positive story from the same city.
questions.explanation: Fact 6 says constructive journalism improves information quality. The near miss is thinking context means ignoring or replacing bad events.

questions.prompt: The local-data designer's Stockholm display shows that several common local guesses are wrong. Which conclusion should she draw before launch?
choices: Local facts deserve the same correction habit as global facts.
Local facts are easier to know, so one clear display should end the issue.
Local facts matter less than global gaps because people live near them.
questions.explanation: Fact 7 says local data can reveal local misconceptions. The error is assuming only global facts need correction or that nearness makes knowledge easy.

questions.prompt: The reviewer updated a chart last month and now treats the worldview issue as solved. Which response fits the maintenance claim?
choices: She should archive the chart as proof that the team already learned the correction.
She should keep a routine for checking facts, sources, and categories again.
She should wait for a major error before reopening the team's assumptions.
questions.explanation: Fact 9 says factfulness is maintenance. A corrected chart can go stale; waiting for a major error lets the old story rebuild.

questions.prompt: A teacher community shares one reusable misconception test and one lecture script. Which tool best fits the teaching point here?
choices: The lecture script fits best because it delivers the updated facts without a messy guess.
The lecture script fits best because a single clear explanation prevents repeated errors.
The misconception test fits best because learners practice seeing and correcting the old answer.
questions.explanation: Fact 1 supports reusable classroom materials, and the mechanism is practice with feedback. A lecture may inform, but it does not by itself rehearse correction.

reviewCards.front: What changes when factfulness becomes a practice instead of a slogan?
reviewCards.back: It moves from admiring better facts to using routines. A person asks where a claim came from, counts what appears, and updates a lesson, story, plan, or reply before the old picture hardens.

reviewCards.front: How does Gapminder Teach make misconceptions useful in a classroom?
reviewCards.back: Gapminder Teach gives free teaching materials and a teacher community for starting with visible guesses. Students compare those guesses with data, so they practice updating instead of only hearing a correction.

reviewCards.front: Why do Friedman and Zakaria matter for business geography here?
reviewCards.back: Thomas L. Friedman 2005 and Fareed Zakaria 2008 help break the old West-to-Rest map. Bangladesh and Cambodia textiles show why skills, wages, and consumers must be tracked as they move.

reviewCards.front: What does the Atlas of Economic Complexity add to a diversification plan?
reviewCards.back: It makes the team look at current industries and skills before naming the next bet. A country cannot build every bold idea at once; nearby capabilities make some moves more plausible.

reviewCards.front: Recall the fear instinct (Ch 4): in the journalist's draft, how does opening with the frightening event distort the reader's picture before context arrives?
reviewCards.back: The journalist's bad local event is the clearest moment. Constructive journalism adds trend, scale, or local comparison so one vivid story does not feel like the whole pattern.

reviewCards.front: Why does Tim Berners-Lee's linked-data idea fit the practice chapter?
reviewCards.back: Tim Berners-Lee TED 2009 points to checking as a public habit. When a reader can follow source paths behind Gapminder bubble graphs, the chart becomes something to inspect, not just trust.

implementationPlan.title: Ask, Count, Update
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice catching a stale assumption while it is still small. Ask one real person what fact you may be treating as settled, count the assumption you hear in your own reply, then update one sentence before it travels.

ifThenPlans.context: When a correction feels like it needs only one clear explanation
ifThenPlans.plan: If one explanation feels sufficient, then Ask, Count, Update by asking for a first guess and counting how many old answers appear.

ifThenPlans.context: When a market plan uses West and Rest as the map
ifThenPlans.plan: If the map splits rich sellers from poorer buyers, then Ask, Count, Update by counting which income levels now hold skills, wages, and customers.

ifThenPlans.context: When a bad story makes context sound like denial
ifThenPlans.plan: If context feels like softening the truth, then Ask, Count, Update by adding one trend or base rate beside the hard event.

ifThenPlans.context: When a fact check from last month feels permanently settled
ifThenPlans.plan: If the old correction feels done forever, then Ask, Count, Update by checking one source date before repeating the claim.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Listen to your own wording on your next reply about a fact, and count the stale assumptions hiding inside it. Tally them, then rewrite a single sentence to match what is true now.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: For one week, keep a running list of claims that lean on an old map, a single scary story, or a fixed country label. At the end, pick the pattern you saw most and rewrite one example of it in your own words.

memorableLines.text: A habit outlasts a headline.
memorableLines.why: It compresses the hard edge into one plain contrast.

memorableLines.text: Markets move when skills and incomes move.
memorableLines.why: It makes the business geography lesson portable.

memorableLines.why: It links the data infrastructure case to public practice.
